Portable flow · every step and its source
  1. Emit Mojo for native routines

    IN: MGP plan plus imports → Finalize marked device graphs if present; EmitMojo produces routine source. OUT: Kernel IR preparation includes imports from P1. ↗ GraphCompiler.cpp:382 ↗ JitCompileKernels.cpp:547

    Why: The runtime plan and the native implementation have separate representations.

  2. Select the host compiler, then check code cache

    IN: Generated routines and target/compiler options → Convert LIT→KGEN, create host ObjectCompiler, then check reusable compiled resources. OUT: Miss follows elaboration; hit can reuse bytes/symbol names. ↗ JitCompileKernels.cpp:575 ↗ JitCompileKernels.cpp:586 ↗ JitCompileKernels.cpp:248

    Why: Reuse avoids regenerating identical native code, not runtime buffers.

  3. Specialize and isolate GPU offload

    IN: P1 bodies; BN=16,BD=8,dtype=f32,rank=2,target=gpu → runElaborationPipeline specializes KGEN and isolates the device kernel module. OUT: Host routine IR and separate GPU kernel IR. ↗ JitCompileKernels.cpp:440 ↗ KGENCompiler.cpp:610

    Why: CPU orchestration and GPU arithmetic target different machines.

  4. Lower LLVM dialect; translate to LLVM IR

    IN: Specialized host/device modules → ObjectCompiler runs lowering; translateModuleToLLVMIR builds llvm::Module. OUT: Native LLVM IR for each target. ↗ ObjectCompiler.cpp:807 ↗ KGENCompiler.cpp:720

    Why: LLVM dialect is MLIR; target backends consume LLVM IR.

  5. Emit target device image D1

    IN: GPU LLVM IR with triple/architecture/features → NVIDIA: LLVM emits PTX; CUDA compiler obtains cubin. OUT: D1 GPU image bytes in host memory. ↗ NVPTXBackend.cpp:154 ↗ NVPTXBackend.cpp:204

    Why: Device instructions must match the selected GPU target.

  6. Emit host code resource A1

    IN: Host routine module and device payload references → ObjectCompiler::emitArchive produces native host resource bytes. OUT: A1 bytes + generated host symbol list. ↗ ObjectCompiler.cpp:1023

    Why: The runtime later resolves host callables from these resources.

  7. Turn compiled calls into runtime primitives

    IN: MGP plan; A1 and generated symbols → LowerCompiledRoutines inserts ModuleLoad / ExecuteGeneric. OUT: init loads by symbol; execute calls by module/function indexes. ↗ LowerCompiledRoutines.cpp:102

    Why: Loading can happen once while data calls repeat.

  8. Serialize the runtime artifact

    IN: Final runtime functions and resources → convertMOToMEF serializes the program and resources. OUT: MEF bytes retained by native compiled artifact. ↗ FrameworkFrontend.cpp:371

    Why: The result no longer depends on running Python graph-recording statements.

  9. Return C1 after compilation succeeds

    IN: Resolved compile result → Synchronous compile waits and returns CompiledModel. OUT: C1._compiled + expected_weights={} + graph names. ↗ api.py:1112 ↗ api.py:442

    Why: init now has an artifact to bind to runtime services.

What selects the backend?

The host routine uses the CPU process's target. Each device offload has its own target triple, architecture and feature options. For NVIDIA a representative triple is nvptx64-nvidia-cuda; an architecture such as sm_90a is an example setting, not the GPU detected for this document. For AMD the corresponding example is amdgcn-amd-amdhsa with gfx942. The compiler registry maps the triple to a backend implementation; LLVM's target machinery then generates instructions appropriate to the target. ↗ ObjectCompiler.cpp:146 ↗ KGENCompiler.cpp:720

.text and .data are sections, not tensors

An ELF section table organizes code, constants, writable globals, symbols and relocations for tools. A program-header table describes segments for loading executable/shared objects; a PT_LOAD segment can cover several sections. Relocatable host objects are handled by JITLink's object/link-graph machinery. NVIDIA cubin and AMD HSA code objects carry vendor-specific GPU code and metadata; their vendor loaders manage the final device resources. ↗ ExecutionEngine.cpp:246 ↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:2262 ↗ HIPDeviceContext.cpp:1968 ↗ System V ABI · ELF program loading ↗ NVIDIA · CUDA binary utilities ↗ LLVM · AMDGPU code objects and kernel dispatch

A1 bytes in host memory                 D1 bytes in host memory
  code + constants + symbol references    code + kernel metadata + symbols
                ↓ JITLink                         ↓ CUDA / HIP loader
host executable mappings → H1          device executable resources → KD1

Q/K/V/O allocations are a separate runtime path.

Why two compilers and two loaders?

The CPU must call runtime services and obey a host ABI. The GPU must execute a device kernel with its own data layout, address spaces and calling convention. Their artifacts cannot be exchanged merely because both use ELF containers. The host object may retain embedded image bytes or resource references for D1; exact section names/placement require inspecting emitted artifacts for a concrete compiler configuration. ↗ KGENCompiler.cpp:610 ↗ device_context.mojo:3151

Files versus memory

emitArchive names a compiler API returning a code buffer; the current StaticArchiveLayer registers an object interface/materialization unit. This does not prove a conventional .a containing multiple members. export_mef(path) would write C1 to disk, but the source calls only compile/init. The normal route needs no explicit .so for every kernel. ↗ StaticArchiveLayer.cpp:108 ↗ api.py:449

  3. Check existing namespace

    IN: Hash key → addIfAbsent checks under a mutex. OUT: Existing namespace reused or new registration begins. ↗ ExecutionEngine.h:159

    Why: Avoid duplicate registration in this execution engine.

  4. Read the object interface

    IN: Owned object bytes → getObjectFileInterface reads definitions/flags. OUT: Symbol interface, with addresses still pending. ↗ StaticArchiveLayer.cpp:108

    Why: Names can be registered before code is materialized.

  5. Define a materialization unit

    IN: Interface + object buffer → dylib.define stores the unit with resource tracker. OUT: Object ready for lazy symbol materialization. ↗ StaticArchiveLayer.cpp:111

    Why: Separate availability of a symbol from its memory address.

    IN: Requested generated host symbol → Lookup asks the unit to emit into ObjectLinkingLayer. OUT: Object enters JITLink. ↗ CompiledKernelsContext.cpp:166 ↗ StaticArchiveLayer.cpp:53

    Why: H1 must become callable before the load completes.

    Why: Instructions need executable storage, separate from tensor buffers.

  8. Resolve and finalize

    IN: Link graph + external symbol definitions → LLVM resolves references, applies relocations, finalizes memory. OUT: Ready host instruction address H1. ↗ ExecutionEngine.cpp:246 ↗ LLVM · ORCv2 design

    Why: A named call/reference must resolve to a valid target address.

    Why: The generated .so is not libcuda and is not D1.

The final protection/relocation work crosses into LLVM. ↗ ExecutionEngine.cpp:197 ↗ ExecutionEngine.cpp:246 ↗ LLVM · ORCv2 design

Why JITDylib does not mean dlopen

An ORC JITDylib is a symbol namespace and dependency/search unit. Ordinary A1 loading builds one in memory. By contrast, the debug path explicitly writes .o, generates .so with the configured linker, and uses a dynamic-library search generator. Installed libcuda.so.1 or HIP libraries are yet another category: vendor runtime dependencies, not outputs of session.compile. ↗ CompiledKernelsContext.cpp:144 ↗ CompiledKernelsContext.cpp:152 ↗ CUDADriver.cpp:61 ↗ HIPDriver.cpp:60

Why the engine must outlive the model's work

The code mappings, symbol namespaces and retained source bytes belong to the execution engine/layers. MGP state holds references to CompiledKernelsContext. A task still executing H1 cannot tolerate the engine freeing that code. The header makes the lifetime requirement explicit. Returning a Python Buffer does not grant ownership of the executable memory to that Buffer. ↗ CompiledKernelsContext.h:141 ↗ StaticArchiveLayer.cpp:95

What is passed to the loader?

moduleName   = compiler-generated module identity
functionName = compiler-generated device entry symbol
code         = D1 cubin bytes (NVIDIA) or HSA code-object bytes (AMD)
context      = S1's selected GPU device context
result       = device-module handle MD1 + kernel-function handle KD1

The code bytes are already prepared by the device backend in the traced compile path. The CUDA module API also supports other image types, but this walkthrough's NVIDIA backend obtains cubin through the compilation device. Source function names and generated entry symbols are not guaranteed to be identical. ↗ NVPTXBackend.cpp:204 ↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:2262

What “place ELF on the GPU” really means

The ELF container remains input to a loader. It describes executable code, symbols, metadata and possibly global data. The driver creates appropriate device resources and returns handles; it need not copy file headers and section tables into an ordinary Q/K/V Buffer. Tensor memory allocations and executable module allocations have separate roles. Exact physical addresses, demand paging and lazy code residency belong to the vendor driver. Module load success does not by itself establish that every code page has been eagerly resident since init. ↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:2262 ↗ NVIDIA CUDA Driver API · module management ↗ NVIDIA · CUDA binary utilities

The native CUDA/HIP driver wrapper locates its installed libraries and resolves entry points. Those library paths may be configurable; a fixed absolute installation path is not assumed. ↗ CUDADriver.cpp:61 ↗ HIPDriver.cpp:107 ↗ CUDACompilationDriver.cpp:49 ↗ CompiledKernelsContext.cpp:133

Why cache by code identity and options?

A same-named kernel can have different specializations or code. Shared-memory/debug/optimization options also affect loading. The cache key includes these distinctions and returns owning references, avoiding driver load/get-function calls on the normal hit branch. Loading is reached when this generated site runs; a selected preload/capture route could run it before ordinary execution. ↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:2217 ↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:2223

Host ABI example

mgp_generic_execute obtains a CompiledKernelAsyncABIFn, whose C++ type is void(void**). It builds an array containing addresses of operand and result AsyncValueRef slots, then constant-resource pointer/size pairs. The generated shim knows how to unpack these values. An input slot can refer to Tensor(shape=[32,32], storage=Q_gpu). A result slot will be fulfilled with the output's runtime value. ↗ CompiledKernelsContext.h:101 ↗ MGPPrimitives.cpp:98

Device argument-pack example

GPU data allocation         host argument storage           driver argument array
Q_gpu, 4096 bytes      ←    slotQ = encoded Q descriptor ←   args[0] = &slotQ
K_gpu, 4096 bytes      ←    slotK = encoded K descriptor ←   args[1] = &slotK
V_gpu, 4096 bytes      ←    slotV = encoded V descriptor ←   args[2] = &slotV
O_gpu, 4096 bytes      ←    slotO = encoded O descriptor ←   args[3] = &slotO

This is a schematic grouping by the four source TileTensor arguments. Exact binary fields and slot count depend on specialization, device layout and compiler lowering. A descriptor can contain a device pointer and shape/layout fields; some properties are compile-time constants. Stack, heap, shared and device memory

StorageExample owner / lifetimePurpose
Host stack / temporary vectorsLaunch helper, until argument values are consumedArgument metadata and slot-address array
Host heap / reference-counted objectsSession/model/task/result ownersRuntime objects, code resources and references
GPU tensor allocationsBuffer owners and outstanding runtime workQ/K/V/O data
GPU module resourcesDriver module/function cache ownersDevice instructions, globals/constants when present
Per-thread private storageKernel executionLocals; register/spill placement is compiler-dependent
Per-block shared storageCooperative work in one block, when the kernel/helpers request itBlock-local sharing; separate from host heap

The kernel's stack_allocation expresses local temporary tensor storage. It does not mean a host CPU stack is transferred to the GPU. Actual register/spill/shared usage must be established from emitted code or device measurement. ↗ fused_attention.mojo:333 ↗ device_context.mojo:3628

Is this RPC? What is host↔GPU IPC?

The shown route has a host call into the installed CUDA/HIP runtime, which submits a device command. It is not an HTTP call, a MAX Serve request, a remote Python function or an RPC to a peer process. Device work is asynchronous offload with kernel arguments and stream ordering. The only separate compiler process in this example's normal preparation path is mojo precompile. ↗ run.py:74 ↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:1610

Below the vendor API, command queues, memory mappings, OS driver interfaces and completion mechanisms connect CPU and GPU. Discrete-GPU data may cross an interconnect; physical transport and placement depend on platform/runtime configuration. AMD's documented AQL queues are one device-dispatch mechanism; this MAX source calls HIP rather than constructing those packets here. CUDA/HIP IPC APIs for sharing resources between processes are separate APIs and are not part of this traced example. ↗ LLVM · AMDGPU code objects and kernel dispatch ↗ NVIDIA CUDA Driver API · execution control

What moves and what remains

For this shape each tensor has 32×32×4 = 4096 bytes. There are three input transfers (12,288 logical bytes) and a 4096-byte output if the reader adds explicit readback. These are tensor payload counts, excluding allocator overhead, protocol traffic, padding and caches. This is arithmetic about the declared shapes, not measured bus traffic. ↗ fused_attention.py:36 ↗ fused_attention.py:78

G1/P1 need not be rebuilt for each call to M1. Code/resources remain with their runtime owners, while each call has data and result lifetimes. Buffer.from_numpy can wrap a contiguous host array without copying; .to(GPU0) requests the device transfer. Native prepareInput then adapts already-device-resident storage without uploading it again. ↗ buffer.py:169 ↗ Buffer.cpp:727 ↗ InferenceSession.cpp:479

Why a CPU task is not a device-completion event

H1 executes CPU instructions that can enqueue GPU work. Host return establishes that this portion of the host routine has returned, not that the entire GPU is idle. Device streams/events and runtime dependencies determine when work and buffers are ready. awaitOrError(results) waits for the result AsyncValues used by result extraction. Buffer host access has its own synchronization path. The exact stream/event details are in the native device backend; do not replace them with an invented global synchronization after every API. ↗ MGPPrimitives.cpp:234 ↗ ModelExecution.cpp:137 ↗ Buffer.cpp:416

Why retain inputs through submission?

The queued primitive owns a closure with operand and output references and a device context. Those objects keep referenced storage/services valid while host work is in progress. The generated routine/runtime associates device operations with their buffer lifetimes. The caller must also obey the API's ownership contract when using external memory. Runtime results may alias; result extraction uses a cache and shallow tensor borrowing to avoid double ownership errors. ↗ MGPPrimitives.cpp:212 ↗ ModelExecution.cpp:151

Initialization readiness versus execution readiness

createExecutableModel already waited for setup before returning M1. This execution path is not the first place that validates a failed initialization. ExecutableModel::execute supplies the initial chain, MGP state, weights and extra init results to the execute function, followed by the user inputs. The weights registry is empty for this example; Q/K/V are not loaded model weights. ↗ EngineContext.cpp:91 ↗ MEFModel.cpp:373

No server or cross-process transport is added

The Python process, MAX runtime workers and vendor user-space API participate locally. This path contains no API server, KV-cache manager, batching service or network protocol. Vendor-driver internals can use mechanisms beyond what is visible here; the animations stop at the documented dispatch/completion boundary instead of presenting physical DMA scheduling as source-proven MAX behavior. ↗ fused_attention.py:23 ↗ ModelExecution.cpp:193

Simplifying MO: concrete comparisons

Canonicalization can remove a supported identity operation, and common-subexpression elimination can share two identical pure computations with identical operands/types. A schematic t1=identity(q); custom(t1,k,v) becomes custom(q,k,v) when the operation's canonicalization permits it. Two identical constant definitions can become one shared constant. Chain canonicalization reduces redundant ordering structure. These illustrate the passes' purpose; the one-custom-call input graph does not demonstrate those exact rewrites, and side-effectful calls cannot be merged just because their names match. ↗ GraphCompiler.cpp:242

MAP access/fusion example

For a separate fusible elementwise chain t=q+1; o=t*2, compatible per-element accesses may let generated code load q[i], compute (q[i]+1)*2, and store o[i] without a materialized intermediate t. That is a comparison explaining why access information is useful. This attention example already implements QK/softmax/PV inside its custom Mojo routine; no claim is made that MAP automatically fuses arbitrary custom calls or splits this routine into those Python operations. ↗ GraphCompiler.cpp:338 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:333

MojoRegistry and MAPToMOGGState

MojoRegistry(module) is a compiler-side view of imported declaration operations, not a running model or Python dict of GPUs. An illustrative lookup is "modular_ops::fused_attention_custom" → declaration for FusedAttention.execute. MAPToMOGGState(registry, op) keeps the lowering context for the current opaque iteration; lowerOp rewrites that operation with selected implementation calls. The resulting “glue” passes shapes, device context, buffer roles and parameters between generated routines. The package registration and tensor signature provide the concrete values. ↗ MAPToMOGG.cpp:57 ↗ MAPToMOGG.cpp:66 ↗ MojoRegistry.cpp:48

JIT means just-in-time compilation

Here session.compile(graph) asks compiler libraries inside the Python process to produce specialized native routines before the first numerical execute. It is still called JIT because native compilation happens as part of program execution. The earlier mojo precompile subprocess only prepares package IR. Kernel cache hits can reuse prepared resource bytes/symbol names; they are not yet resident callable pointers. ↗ JitCompileKernels.cpp:248 ↗ JitCompileKernels.cpp:567

The source checks is_device_graph before device-graph finalization. This Python Graph does not request that option; an ordinary computation graph on a GPU is not automatically a CUDA Graph capture. ↗ graph.py:831 ↗ GraphCompiler.cpp:382

Host linking is a separate mechanism

Normal loading uses ORC/JITLink with an in-process memory mapper. A code section obtains executable host memory; references to other symbols are resolved and relocations applied. The debug branch instead writes an object, invokes the configured linker with -shared, and loads its temporary .so. Both end with host callable lookup. The GPU D1 payload is subsequently loaded through CUDA/HIP APIs. ↗ ExecutionEngine.cpp:197 ↗ CompiledKernelsContext.cpp:119 ↗ CompiledKernelsContext.cpp:144

How the bytes get to the GPU

MAX passes the image bytes to the vendor's module loader. The image has code, symbols and metadata needed by that loader. The driver creates device-specific executable resources and returns opaque handles. MAX does not allocate a tensor Buffer and memcpy the entire ELF file into it as if it were matrix data. Exact physical placement, page mapping and lazy loading are vendor-driver details. ↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:2262 ↗ HIPDeviceContext.cpp:1968

H1 is a host instruction address. MD1 is a device-module handle, KD1 is a kernel-function handle, and Q_gpu is a tensor allocation. Calling cuLaunchKernelEx submits KD1 with a grid, block dimensions, stream and argument pack. The CPU does not directly jump to the GPU instruction pointer. ↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:1610

    Q = [[1,0], [0,1]]          two independent queries

    For query [1,0], scores are [1,0 | 2,0]; the maximum grows from 1 to 2. Tile one has m=1, l=1+exp(-1)=1.367879, and normalized O=[0.731059,0.537883]. Tile two sets alpha=exp(1-2)=0.367879. Old denominator mass becomes 0.503215; new tile mass is 1.135335; new total l=1.638550. The old output's multiplier is alpha*l_old/l_new=0.307110. Current weights are [0.610296,0.082595]. Add their V contribution to the rescaled old output. The browser computes these quantities from the matrices instead of storing rounded captions. ↗ fused_attention.mojo:348 ↗ fused_attention.mojo:366

    Why the old result must be rescaled

    Changing the maximum changes the reference for every exponential, including keys already processed. Changing the denominator changes every normalized weight. Multiplying the retained output by alpha*l_old/l_new accounts for both changes; merely adding a new tile's independently normalized output would be wrong. A second query has its own m/l/O values, so normalizing across all rows together would also be wrong. ↗ fused_attention.mojo:367

    What remains in memory

    Q/K/V/O are global tensor buffers. Each block visits local score and exponential tiles, keeping per-row m/l and a partial output tile across iterations. This example calls stack_allocation for local tile storage; register allocation/spills and actual occupancy require generated-code analysis. The drawing counts logical elements, not measured device memory consumption. No persistent full 32×32 score buffer is requested by this loop. ↗ fused_attention.mojo:333

    The tiny animation uses −∞ as the initial neutral maximum; the source initializes m_1 with Scalar[q_dtype].MIN. For the finite scores in this example, the first tile replaces that sentinel before it contributes mass. The animation is browser arithmetic, not GPU execution or a numerical test of MAX. It follows the same unscaled softmax(QKᵀ)V recurrence. ↗ fused_attention.mojo:335

    7. Optional: copy the result to the host

      IN: Reader-added output[0].to(CPU()).to_numpy() → Request device→host copy and synchronize for host access. OUT: Host-readable float32[32,32] values. ↗ buffer.py:194 ↗ Buffer.cpp:416

      Why: Inspecting matrix contents requires the appropriate storage/readiness boundary.

    Three useful readiness statements

    StatementWhat it establishes
    H1 returnedThe host shim has returned or arranged its result dependencies; this alone is not a global GPU barrier
    awaitOrError(results) succeededThe native result AsyncValues needed by the driver wrapper are available without error
    Buffer synchronization / completed host readbackThe relevant storage can be read by the host under that API's synchronization contract

    GPU streams order work submitted to them; event-based dependencies can coordinate different contexts/streams. AsyncRT chains coordinate the host runtime's execution plan. These mechanisms cooperate, but a chain token is not a tensor and a host condition variable is not an online-softmax denominator. ↗ MGPPrimitives.cpp:176 ↗ ModelExecution.cpp:137 ↗ Buffer.cpp:416

    Why references are retained

    The queued branch can outlive its caller's stack frame. Its closure retains operands, output slots and a device context while H1 runs. It resolves downstream result slots only after releasing context-reachable task references. This prevents a completion observer from tearing down resources that the host task still uses. Returned O1 owns its storage independently of the temporary launch-argument pack. ↗ MGPPrimitives.cpp:212 ↗ MGPPrimitives.cpp:251

    The actual example ends with print(output) and no explicit readback. The optional readback shown here is clearly separated in the animation. ↗ fused_attention.py:83

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from max.driver import CPU, Accelerator, Buffer, accelerator_count
from max.dtype import DType
from max.engine.api import InferenceSession
from max.graph import DeviceRef, Graph, TensorType, ops


def main() -> None:
    mojo_kernels = Path(__file__).parent / "kernels"

    dtype = DType.float32

    # Place the graph on a GPU, if available. Fall back to CPU if not.
    device = CPU() if accelerator_count() == 0 else Accelerator()
    if accelerator_count() == 0:
        N = 8
        D = 8
        BD = 4
        BN = 4
    else:
        N = 32
        D = 32
        BD = 8
        BN = 16

    with Graph(
        "fused_attention",
        input_types=[
            TensorType(
                dtype, shape=[N, D], device=DeviceRef.from_device(device)
            ),
            TensorType(
                dtype, shape=[N, D], device=DeviceRef.from_device(device)
            ),
            TensorType(
                dtype, shape=[N, D], device=DeviceRef.from_device(device)
            ),
        ],
        custom_extensions=[mojo_kernels],
    ) as graph:
        q, k, v, *_ = graph.inputs
        results = ops.custom(
            name="modular_ops::fused_attention_custom",
            device=DeviceRef.from_device(device),
            parameters={"BD": BD, "BN": BN},
            values=[q, k, v],
            out_types=[
                TensorType(
                    dtype, shape=[N, D], device=DeviceRef.from_device(device)
                )
            ],
        )
        graph.output(*results)

    # Set up an inference session for running the graph.
    session = InferenceSession(devices=[device])

    # Compile the graph.
    compiled = session.compile(graph)
    model = session.init(compiled)

    np.random.seed(123)
    Q = Buffer.from_numpy(np.random.randn(N, D).astype("f")).to(device)
    K = Buffer.from_numpy(np.random.randn(N, D).astype("f")).to(device)
    V = Buffer.from_numpy(np.random.randn(N, D).astype("f")).to(device)

    output = model.execute(Q, K, V)
    print(output)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""
The code below computes the attention score for a tile of size BN x BD.
It follows the exact arithmetic as described in the FlashAttention-2 paper
(https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.08691). The variable names in this program
reflect the variable names in the algorithms from the paper.

Here, the following tensors are Q for the query,
K for the key, V for the value, and O for the output.

       Q            K               V
  +----D----+  +----D----+   +--+--BD--+---+
  |         |  |.........|   |  |......|   |
  |         |  |.........|   |  |......|   |
  +---------+  |.........|   |  |......|   |
  |.........|  |.........|   |  |......|   |
  BN........|  N.........|   N  |......|   |
  |.........|  |.........|   |  |......|   |
  +---------+  |.........|   |  |......|   |
  |         |  |.........|   |  |......|   |
  |         |  |.........|   |  |......|   |
  |         |  |.........|   |  |......|   |
  +---------+  +---------+   +--+------+---+

The main trick is in the softmax computation.
As the paper says, S and P are intermediate values.

Let S = Q * K^T  ∈ R^{N, D}
    P = Softmax(S) ∈ R^{N, D}
The attention score is O = P * V ∈ R^{N, D}.

One way to think about this is to consider what happens if we
split the dimensions N in  K, and Q into two tiles: K_1 and K_2, V_1 and V_2.
Then we can incrementally compute the output as follows:
  S_1 = Q * K_1, S_2 = Q * K_2
  O_i = O_{i-1} * renormalization_factor + softmax(S_i) * V_i

This allows for the incremental computation of softmax(S_i) * V_i,
leading to the final output.
"""


from max.gpu.host import DeviceContext
from max.gpu import block_idx
from max.gpu.sync import barrier
from layout import TensorLayout, TileTensor, row_major, stack_allocation
from layout.math import max, sum
from layout.tensor_core import TensorCore

from extensibility import register, InputTensor, OutputTensor

from std.utils import Index


@register("modular_ops::fused_attention_custom")
struct FusedAttention:
    """Registers the `fused_attention_custom` op, allowing python to use it from the `max`
    package.
    """

    @staticmethod
    def execute[
        dtype: DType,
        rank: Int,
        //,  # Forces the previous two params to be inferred from the args
        BN: Int,  # Dimension of blocks to split Q into
        BD: Int,  # Dimension of blocks to split K, V into
        target: StaticString,  # "cpu" or "gpu"
    ](
        output: OutputTensor[dtype=dtype, rank=rank, ...],
        query: InputTensor[dtype=dtype, rank=rank, ...],
        key: InputTensor[dtype=dtype, rank=rank, ...],
        value: InputTensor[dtype=dtype, rank=rank, ...],
        ctx: DeviceContext,
    ) raises:
        comptime assert rank == 2, "rank must be 2"

        # Query tensor
        var Q = query.to_tile_tensor().as_unsafe_any_origin()
        # Key tensor
        var K = key.to_tile_tensor().as_unsafe_any_origin()
        # Value tensor
        var V = value.to_tile_tensor().as_unsafe_any_origin()
        # Attention output tensor
        var O = output.to_tile_tensor().as_unsafe_any_origin()

        comptime if target == "cpu":
            print("Running on CPU")
            fused_attention_cpu[BN, BD](Q, K, V, O)
        else:
            var dev_ctx = ctx
            print("Running on GPU")
            fused_attention_gpu[BN, BD](dev_ctx, Q, K, V, O)


# CustomOpLibrary does not support names with '::' in them currently. Create
# a simple alias so the whisper example works.
@register("fused_attention_custom")
struct FusedAttentionAlias:
    @staticmethod
    def execute[
        dtype: DType,
        rank: Int,
        //,  # Forces the previous two params to be inferred from the args
        BN: Int,  # Dimension of blocks to split Q into
        BD: Int,  # Dimension of blocks to split K, V into
        target: StaticString,  # "cpu" or "gpu"
    ](
        output: OutputTensor[dtype=dtype, rank=rank, ...],
        query: InputTensor[dtype=dtype, rank=rank, ...],
        key: InputTensor[dtype=dtype, rank=rank, ...],
        value: InputTensor[dtype=dtype, rank=rank, ...],
        ctx: DeviceContext,
    ) raises:
        FusedAttention.execute[BN=BN, BD=BD, target=target](
            output, query, key, value, ctx
        )


@inline(.always)
def matmul_b_transpose(
    lhs: TileTensor,
    rhs: TileTensor,
    out res: TileTensor[
        lhs.dtype,
        type_of(row_major[lhs.static_shape[0], rhs.static_shape[0]]()),
        MutUntrackedOrigin,
    ],
):
    res = stack_allocation[lhs.dtype](
        row_major[lhs.static_shape[0], rhs.static_shape[0]]()
    )

    comptime for m in range(lhs.static_shape[0]):
        comptime for n in range(rhs.static_shape[0]):
            res[m, n] = 0.0

            comptime for k in range(lhs.static_shape[1]):
                res[m, n] += rebind[res.ElementType](
                    lhs[m, k].cast[res.dtype]()
                ) * rebind[res.ElementType](rhs[n, k].cast[res.dtype]())


# The bulk of the code below implements what the papers calls
# an "online softmax", which is local to each block.
# The algorithm is described as:
#
# $$$
# m_1 = rowmax(S_1)
# l_1 = rowsum(e^(S_1-m_1))
# P_1 = diag(l_1)^-1 * e^(S_1-m_1)
# O_1 = P_1*V_1 = diag(l_1)^-1 * e^(S_1-m_1) * V_1
# m_2 = max(m_1, rowmax(S_2)) = m
# l_2 = e^(m_1-m_2) * l_1 _ rowsum(e^(S_2-m_2))
#     = rowsum(e^(S_1-m)) + rowsum(e^(S_2-m)) = ls
# P_2 = diag(l_2)^-1 * e^(S_2-m_2)
# O_2 = diag(l_1/l_2)^-1 * O_1 + (P_2 * V_2)
#     = diag(l_2)^-1 * e^(S_2-m) * V
# $$$


@inline(.always)
def fused_attention_cpu[
    BN: Int, BD: Int
](Q: TileTensor, K: TileTensor, V: TileTensor, O: TileTensor[mut=True, ...],):
    comptime N = K.static_shape[0]
    comptime D = K.static_shape[1]

    comptime for tile_n in range(N // BN):
        var Q_tile = Q.tile[BN, D](tile_n, 0)

        comptime for tile_d in range(D // BD):
            var m_1 = stack_allocation[Q.dtype](row_major[BN]()).fill(
                Scalar[Q.dtype].MIN
            )

            var l_1 = stack_allocation[Q.dtype](row_major[BN]()).fill(0)

            var O_i = stack_allocation[Q.dtype](row_major[BN, BD]()).fill(0)

            comptime for tile_n_idx in range(N // BN):
                var K_tile = K.tile[BN, D](tile_n_idx, 0)
                var V_tile = V.tile[BN, BD](tile_n_idx, tile_d)

                var S = matmul_b_transpose(Q_tile, K_tile)
                var m_2 = stack_allocation[Q.dtype](row_major[BN]())
                max[axis=1](S, m_2)
                m_2.max(m_1)

                # l_2 = exp(m_1 - m_2) * l_1 + sum(axis=1, exp(S - m_2))
                var l_2 = stack_allocation[Q.dtype](row_major[BN]())
                l_2.copy_from(m_1)
                l_2 -= m_2
                l_2.exp()
                l_2 *= l_1
                var E = stack_allocation[Q.dtype](row_major[BN, BN]())
                E.copy_from(S)
                E -= m_2
                E.exp()
                var l_2_sum = stack_allocation[Q.dtype](row_major[BN]())
                sum[axis=1](E, l_2_sum)
                l_2 += l_2_sum

                # P = exp(S - m_2) / l_2
                E /= l_2
                O_i *= l_1
                O_i /= l_2
                var m_1_delta = stack_allocation[Q.dtype](row_major[BN]())
                m_1_delta.copy_from(m_1)
                m_1_delta -= m_2
                m_1_delta.exp()
                O_i *= m_1_delta
                var PV = matmul["cpu"](E, V_tile)
                O_i += PV
                m_1.copy_from(m_2)
                l_1.copy_from(l_2)

            O.tile[BN, BD](tile_n, tile_d).copy_from(O_i)


@inline(.always)
def matmul[
    dtype: DType,
    rhs_dtype: DType,
    //,
    target: StaticString,
    transpose_b: Bool = False,
](
    lhs: TileTensor[dtype, ...],
    rhs: TileTensor[rhs_dtype, ...],
    out res: TileTensor[
        dtype,
        type_of(row_major[lhs.static_shape[0], rhs.static_shape[0]]()),
        MutUntrackedOrigin,
        address_space=lhs.address_space,
    ],
):
    res = stack_allocation[dtype, address_space=lhs.address_space](
        row_major[lhs.static_shape[0], rhs.static_shape[0]]()
    )

    comptime if target == "cpu":
        comptime for m in range(lhs.static_shape[0]):
            comptime for n in range(rhs.static_shape[1]):
                res[m, n] = 0.0

                comptime for k in range(lhs.static_shape[1]):
                    res[m, n] += rebind[res.ElementType](
                        lhs[m, k].cast[res.dtype]()
                    ) * rebind[res.ElementType](rhs[k, n].cast[res.dtype]())
    else:
        comptime M = lhs.static_shape[0]
        comptime N = rhs.static_shape[0]
        comptime K = lhs.static_shape[1]

        var out_sram = stack_allocation[res.dtype, address_space=.SHARED](
            row_major[M, N]()
        )

        comptime BK = 8

        comptime assert K % 8 == 0, "K needs to be a multiple of 8"

        var mma_b_t = TensorCore[dtype, dtype, Index(M, N, BK), transpose_b]()

        var c_reg = stack_allocation[dtype, address_space=.LOCAL](
            mma_b_t.c_fragment_layout
        ).fill(0)

        # `TensorCore`'s native loads require matching operand dtypes;
        # rebind the B view once when `rhs` carries a different dtype.
        var rhs_typed = rebind[
            TileTensor[
                dtype,
                rhs.LayoutType,
                rhs.origin,
                Engine=rhs.Engine,
                address_space=rhs.address_space,
                linear_idx_type=rhs.linear_idx_type,
            ]
        ](rhs)

        comptime for k_i in range(K // BK):
            var a_reg = mma_b_t.load_a(lhs.tile[M, BK](0, k_i))

            var b_reg = mma_b_t.load_b(rhs_typed.tile[BK, N](k_i, 0))

            comptime if transpose_b:
                b_reg = rebind[type_of(b_reg)](
                    mma_b_t.load_b(rhs_typed.tile[N, BK](0, k_i))
                )

            var d_reg = mma_b_t.mma_op(a_reg, b_reg, c_reg)
            c_reg.copy_from(d_reg)
        mma_b_t.store_d(out_sram, c_reg)

        barrier()
        res.copy_from(out_sram)


def fused_attention_kernel[
    q_dtype: DType,
    q_layout: TensorLayout,
    k_dtype: DType,
    k_layout: TensorLayout,
    v_dtype: DType,
    v_layout: TensorLayout,
    o_dtype: DType,
    o_layout: TensorLayout,
    BN: Int,
    BD: Int,
](
    Q: TileTensor[q_dtype, q_layout, MutAnyOrigin],
    K: TileTensor[k_dtype, k_layout, MutAnyOrigin],
    V: TileTensor[v_dtype, v_layout, MutAnyOrigin],
    O: TileTensor[o_dtype, o_layout, MutAnyOrigin],
):
    comptime N = Q.static_shape[0]
    comptime D = Q.static_shape[1]

    var Q_tile = Q.tile[BN, D](block_idx.y, 0)

    var m_1 = stack_allocation[q_dtype](row_major[BN]()).fill(
        Scalar[q_dtype].MIN
    )
    var l_1 = stack_allocation[q_dtype](row_major[BN]()).fill(0)
    var O_i = stack_allocation[q_dtype](row_major[BN, BD]()).fill(0)

    comptime BN_1 = 8

    for tile_n_idx in range(N // BN_1):
        var K_tile = K.tile[BN_1, D](tile_n_idx, 0)
        var V_tile = V.tile[BN_1, BD](tile_n_idx, block_idx.x)
        var S = matmul["gpu", transpose_b=True](Q_tile, K_tile)
        var m_2 = stack_allocation[q_dtype](row_major[BN]())
        max[axis=1](S, m_2)
        m_2.max(m_1)

        # l_2 = exp(m_1 - m_2) * l_1 + sum(axis=1, exp(S - m_2))
        var l_2 = stack_allocation[q_dtype](row_major[BN]())
        l_2.copy_from(m_1)
        l_2 -= m_2
        l_2.exp()
        l_2 *= l_1
        var E = stack_allocation[q_dtype](row_major[BN, BN_1]())
        E.copy_from(S)
        E -= m_2
        E.exp()
        var l_2_sum = stack_allocation[q_dtype](row_major[BN]())
        sum[axis=1](E, l_2_sum)
        l_2 += l_2_sum

        # P = exp(S - m_2) / l_2
        E /= l_2
        O_i *= l_1
        O_i /= l_2
        var m_1_delta = stack_allocation[q_dtype](row_major[BN]())
        m_1_delta.copy_from(m_1)
        m_1_delta -= m_2
        m_1_delta.exp()
        O_i *= m_1_delta
        var PV = matmul["gpu"](E, V_tile)
        O_i += PV
        m_1.copy_from(m_2)
        l_1.copy_from(l_2)
    O.tile[BN, BD](block_idx.y, block_idx.x).copy_from(O_i)


def fused_attention_gpu[
    BN: Int,
    BD: Int,
](
    ctx: DeviceContext,
    Q: TileTensor,
    K: TileTensor,
    V: TileTensor,
    O: TileTensor[mut=True, ...],
) raises:
    comptime kernel_func = fused_attention_kernel[
        Q.dtype,
        Q.LayoutType,
        K.dtype,
        K.LayoutType,
        V.dtype,
        V.LayoutType,
        O.dtype,
        O.LayoutType,
        BN,
        BD,
    ]
    ctx.enqueue_function[kernel_func](
        Q,
        K,
        V,
        O,
        grid_dim=(Int(Q.dim[1]()) // BD, Int(Q.dim[0]()) // BN),
        block_dim=(32),
    )

    Read on November 12, 2026. General mechanisms inform the original diagrams; the pinned source determines which path this example takes.

    • Bazel · phases of a build

      Bazel separates loading, target analysis and action execution. The local Starlark macro establishes this example’s dependencies.

    • NVIDIA CUDA Driver API · module management

      The module API accepts prepared image bytes, returns module/function handles and documents lazy-loading behavior. Physical placement remains driver-managed.

    • NVIDIA CUDA Driver API · execution control

      The launch API receives launch dimensions, a function and stream, and pointers to argument storage. Enqueue and completion are separate events.

    • NVIDIA · CUDA binary utilities

      A cubin uses ELF to carry CUDA executable code and associated information; it is distinct from the host runtime library.

    • LLVM · AMDGPU code objects and kernel dispatch

      AMDHSA ELF metadata and dispatch conventions define GPU code-object and kernel-argument responsibilities. The MAX example reaches them through HIP.

    • System V ABI · ELF program loading

      Sections organize object contents; program headers describe loadable segments. A loadable segment can have a zero-filled tail beyond its file bytes.

    • LLVM · ORCv2 design

      ORC symbol materialization and JITLink separate registration, symbol resolution and executable-memory finalization.
